summary: The State of the Union is the President's address to a joint session of Congress, fulfilling Article II, Section 3 of the U.S. Constitution. It reports on the nation's condition and lays out the President's legislative agenda and priorities. For much of the first century it was a written report; Woodrow Wilson revived in-person delivery in 1913, and radio and television now broadcast it live.
one_line: The State of the Union is the President's constitutionally grounded address to Congress, reporting on the nation and outlining policy, delivered in person since Wilson in 1913.
key_facts: The State of the Union address fulfills Article II, Section 3 of the U.S. Constitution, which requires the President to periodically inform Congress of the state of the union and recommend measures he judges necessary and expedient.
The address is presented by the President of the United States to a joint session of Congress, except in the first year of a new president's term.
The address lets the President outline his legislative agenda, for which he needs Congress's cooperation, and national priorities.
During most of the country's first century, the President primarily only submitted a written report to Congress.
George Washington delivered the first regular annual message before a joint session of Congress on January 8, 1790, in New York City, then the provisional U.S. capital.
In 1801, Thomas Jefferson discontinued delivering the address in person, regarding it as too monarchical, similar to the Speech from the Throne.
After Jefferson, the address was written and sent to Congress to be read by a clerk until 1913.
Woodrow Wilson, the 28th U.S. President, re-established the in-person address in 1913 despite some initial controversy, as a way to rally support for his agenda.
With the advent of radio and television, the address is now broadcast live across the country on many networks.
Some presidents in the latter half of the 20th century sent written State of the Union addresses.
The last President to send a written address was Jimmy Carter in 1981, after his defeat by Ronald Reagan and days before his term ended.
